before.content_html:
Equipped to Conquer

A Roman legionary in the Imperial period was one of the best-equipped soldiers in the ancient world. His weapons and armour were the product of centuries of refinement, shaped by hard experience in wars against enemies who fought in very different ways. Understanding the legionary’s kit connects directly to understanding how Rome fought and won an empire — and the material evidence for this equipment survives in sculptures, coins, and the objects themselves.

Offensive Weapons: the Gladius and Pilum

The legionary’s primary weapon was the gladius. Unlike Greek or Celtic swords designed for slashing, the gladius was a short, double-edged weapon used primarily for thrusting. In the close press of battle, where there was no room for wide swings, a short stabbing sword was devastatingly effective. The gladius gave the legionary a decisive advantage once the enemy’s formation had been broken.

Before closing with the sword, the legionary threw a heavy javelin known as the pilum. The pilum was a remarkable piece of engineering: a wooden shaft with a long iron shank topped by a small pyramidal head. The iron shank was deliberately thin so that it would bend or snap on impact, wedging into the enemy’s shield and weighing it down. Even if the pilum did not wound its target, the stricken shield became a liability that the enemy had to discard before he could fight effectively. A volley of pila delivered just before the charge created shock, disorder and disadvantage in the opposing line.

Key Fact

The legionary fought with three weapons in sequence: the pilum (heavy javelin thrown to disrupt the enemy line), the gladius (short stabbing sword for close combat), and a pugio (dagger for last resort). Each weapon served a specific tactical purpose in the Roman system of fighting.

Defensive Equipment: Shield and Armour

The legionary’s large rectangular shield, the scutum, was one of his most important pieces of equipment. In the Imperial period, the scutum was typically semi-cylindrical in shape, curving around the soldier’s body to protect his left side. Made from layers of wood glued at right angles (a technique similar to modern plywood), covered in leather and linen, with a metal boss at the centre, it was both strong and relatively lightweight. The boss could be used offensively to punch and knock opponents off balance.

The body was protected by lorica segmentata. This articulated armour was constructed from overlapping strips of iron plate, connected by leather straps and brass fittings. It was flexible enough to allow the wearer to move, crouch and fight, yet strong enough to deflect sword cuts and arrows. The head was protected by a close-fitting iron helmet with a neckguard, cheekpieces and a brow-plate to deflect downward blows. The bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum gives a clear visual record of how these elements combined in the soldier’s overall appearance.

The combination of pilum, gladius and scutum was designed to produce a specific fighting method. Soldiers advanced in close formation, locked shields to form a wall, threw their pila at the last moment, then pushed into the disordered enemy with their gladii. The tortoise formation (testudo) showed the scutum’s versatility: used during sieges, soldiers locked shields above their heads and on all sides to create a near-impenetrable shell against arrows and thrown stones. The equipment and the tactics were inseparable — remove one element and the whole system was weakened.

The Marching Camp

One of the most remarkable things about the Roman army was not what it did in battle but what it built every single night on campaign. The Roman marching camp was a fully fortified enclosure constructed at the end of each day’s march. Vegetius, writing in the late Roman period, describes the procedure clearly: the camp had a standard rectangular layout, with gates on all four sides, a rampart and ditch on the perimeter, and a regular internal arrangement of tents and streets that meant every soldier knew exactly where to go.

The rampart was built from the earth dug out of the surrounding ditch. The ditch was V-shaped, typically around 1.5 metres wide and approximately 0.9 metres deep (five Roman feet wide and three Roman feet deep, as described by the military writer Vegetius), making it difficult to cross under fire. On top of the rampart, soldiers planted sharpened stakes that they carried as part of their standard marching kit. This combination of ditch, rampart and stakes created a defensible perimeter in just a few hours. The ability to fortify a position every night meant a Roman army could never be caught completely unprepared by a night attack — a huge strategic advantage.

Key Fact

The Roman marching camp was a temporary fortified enclosure built every evening on campaign. It had a rectangular layout, a perimeter ditch, a rampart built from the excavated earth, and sharpened stakes on top. The Roman fortress at Chester grew out of this temporary camp tradition into a permanent installation.

Roman engineering extended to siege warfare. When faced with a fortified town, the legion could construct a full siege complex: approach ramps of earth and timber, artillery platforms for ballistae (bolt-throwing machines) and onagri (stone-throwing catapults), and covered corridors to advance soldiers under missile fire. Trajan’s Column in Rome, which depicts the emperor’s campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century AD, is a richly detailed carved relief running in a spiral around the column shaft. Among its many scenes are soldiers building camps, bridging rivers, operating artillery and conducting assaults — making it one of the most comprehensive visual sources we have for Roman military practice.

Rome at War

Rome did not acquire its empire by accident. Over five centuries of nearly continuous warfare, the Roman army developed and adapted tactics, organisation and technology that allowed it to defeat opponents as varied as Macedonian phalanxes, Celtic warbands, desert guerrillas and Eastern cavalry. This lesson focuses on Roman warfare in the Imperial period and on two key conflicts: Trajan’s campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century AD, and the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC that determined who would rule the Roman world.

Tactics and Adaptability

The Roman army’s greatest strength was its capacity to adapt. When facing enemies who excelled in archery, Rome recruited auxiliary archers from Syria. When fighting desert nomads, it reorganised supply lines. The fundamental tactical approach, however, was consistent: use the pilum volley to disorder the enemy, close to sword range, and overwhelm with disciplined pressure from the scutum-wall.

Roman generals understood that battle was often decided before it started — by choosing ground, by tiring the enemy, by cutting off supply lines. The logistics of a Roman campaign were extraordinary: granaries at fortresses along the Rhine and Danube, a network of roads that allowed rapid troop movements, and a river fleet that carried supplies deep into enemy territory. Trajan’s Column records this infrastructure vividly — among its carved scenes are soldiers unloading supplies from boats and engineers constructing pontoon bridges.

Key Fact

Trajan fought two major campaigns against the Dacians: the First Dacian War (101–102 AD) and the Second Dacian War (105–106 AD). Both are recorded in detail on Trajan’s Column in Rome and commemorated on the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — two of the most important prescribed visual sources for Roman warfare.

Trajan’s Dacian Campaigns

Dacia, roughly equivalent to modern Romania, was a powerful kingdom north of the Danube ruled by a capable king named Decebalus. Decebalus had humiliated Rome in previous conflicts, extracting tribute money and capturing Roman prisoners. Trajan invaded in 101 AD to recover Roman prestige and to seize Dacian gold reserves that were among the largest in the ancient world. The first war ended with Decebalus surrendering and agreeing to Roman terms; when he broke those terms, Trajan launched a second, more brutal campaign that ended with the destruction of the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa and Decebalus’s suicide rather than capture.

Trajan’s Column, standing in Rome, is a hollow marble column roughly 30 metres tall, around whose shaft winds a continuous carved relief depicting both campaigns in over 150 individual scenes. The column begins with river-gods and troops crossing a pontoon bridge and moves through sieges, battle scenes, negotiations and triumphal processions to the final conquest. The Arch of Trajan at Benevento, a triumphal arch decorated with relief panels, shows Trajan receiving submission from Dacian enemies, distributing grain to Roman citizens, and associating his victories with divine favour. Both monuments present the campaigns as evidence of Roman greatness and Trajan’s exceptional leadership.

Trajan’s Column is an invaluable source for Roman military practice — it shows fort construction, river crossings, artillery use, allied auxiliary troops and siege operations in remarkable detail. However, it was a piece of state propaganda. Trajan is always shown in a commanding position; Roman soldiers are always disciplined and orderly. The Dacians are depicted as brave enemies to make the conquest more impressive, but they are also shown in defeat and submission. The column does not show Roman atrocities, looting or the suffering of civilian populations — it presents an idealised narrative of Roman power. Students must weigh this selectivity when using the column as evidence.

Siege Warfare

Roman success against fortified towns and hillfort strongholds depended on specialised siege techniques. The standard approach involved surrounding the enemy position with a circumvallation — a wall or ditch that encircled the entire position and cut off all resupply. This was then supplemented by direct assault: battering rams mounted in wheeled towers, artillery firing stones and bolts, and approach ramps of earth built up to the level of the enemy walls. Trajan’s Column shows all of these techniques in use against Dacian hillforts.

The Battle of Actium, 31 BC

The naval battle of Actium was fought off the coast of north-western Greece on 2 September 31 BC. On one side was Octavian (the future Augustus) commanding a fleet under his brilliant admiral Marcus Agrippa. On the other were the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII of Egypt. The battle decided who would control the entire Roman world. Octavian’s victory made him undisputed master of Rome and led directly to the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The trireme had been the dominant warship of the classical Greek period, but by Actium the principal warships were larger vessels called quinqueremes and triremes built on a grander scale. Agrippa’s fleet used grappling hooks and boarding tactics to neutralise Antony’s heavier ships. When Cleopatra’s squadron broke off the engagement and retreated towards Egypt, Antony followed — and his remaining fleet, left without leadership, surrendered. The battle showed that naval supremacy could decide the fate of an entire empire.

Key Fact

The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeat the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. The victory is commemorated by a relief in the Vatican Museum and on the shield depicted on the Augustus of Prima Porta statue, where the scene of Actium is carved in miniature on the emperor’s breastplate armour.

The Romans invested enormous effort in commemorating military victory in permanent public form. Triumphal arches — like the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — were built at key road entry points so that every traveller would be reminded of Roman greatness. Victory columns like Trajan’s Column placed the narrative of a campaign literally at the heart of the city, in the forum that bore the emperor’s name. Coins were struck to broadcast the victory to every corner of the empire: the Mark Antony Legionary denarius (minted c. 32 BC) shows a warship on the obverse and an eagle between two military standards on the reverse, advertising his naval and military strength to his soldiers. Even defeat was commemorated: Augustus recovered the eagles lost by Varus in the Teutoburg Forest disaster (9 AD) decades later and displayed them publicly as proof that Rome always demanded and achieved satisfaction.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Trajan fought two Dacian campaigns (101–102 AD and 105–106 AD); both are recorded on Trajan’s Column and the Arch of Trajan at Benevento, which are key prescribed visual sources presenting victories as imperial propaganda.
  • The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet defeat Antony and Cleopatra, making Octavian master of the Roman world and leading to the creation of the Roman Empire under Augustus.
  • Roman military success rested on adaptable tactics, engineering capability (camps, siege works, roads) and the political use of commemorative monuments to project Roman power.

before.content_html:
The Ideal of the Warrior

In both Greek and Roman culture, the warrior was not simply a fighter — he was a moral exemplar. How a man behaved in battle was seen as the truest test of his character. The values associated with military heroism — courage, endurance, loyalty to comrades and willingness to die for one’s community — were celebrated in literature, memorialised in public monuments and held up as ideals that every free male citizen should aspire to. Understanding these values is essential for interpreting the literary and visual sources for warfare.

Greek Values of War: Honour and Shame

Greek war culture was built on the concepts of kleos (glory) and time (honour). A warrior who fought bravely and died well won kleos that would outlive him — his name would be remembered in song and story. A warrior who fled the field, discarded his shield, or surrendered brought lasting shame not only on himself but on his family and community. This culture of shame is expressed powerfully in the Spartan saying attributed to mothers sending sons to war: “Come back with your shield, or on it” — meaning either victorious or dead, but never in flight.

The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus expressed this value system with striking force. His Fragment 10, known as ‘The Fallen Warrior’, is one of the prescribed literary sources. In it, Tyrtaeus argues that dying in the front rank of battle is the finest thing a young man can do. He contrasts the eternal glory of the fallen warrior with the misery of the exile who wanders as a beggar, dishonoured and unwelcome everywhere. For Tyrtaeus, dying bravely for Sparta is not just admirable — it is the only thing that makes a life worthwhile. The poem was designed to be performed at syssitia (communal dining halls where Spartan soldiers ate and trained together), keeping the ideal of heroic self-sacrifice constantly present in the warrior community.

Key Fact

Tyrtaeus’s Fragment 10 (‘The Fallen Warrior’) is a Spartan poem that celebrates dying in battle as the highest honour. It contrasts the glory of the man who dies in the front rank with the shame and misery of the man who abandons his position. It was performed at Spartan communal meals to reinforce the warrior ideal.

Heroism at Thermopylae

The values expressed by Tyrtaeus found their most famous embodiment at the battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC. The Spartan king Leonidas and roughly three hundred Spartan warriors, along with several thousand allied troops, held the narrow mountain pass against the vast Persian army of Xerxes for three days. When the Spartan ally Ephialtes showed the Persians a path around the pass, Leonidas sent away the allied contingents and remained with his Spartans and a few Thespians and Thebans to fight to the death. According to Herodotus, when told that Persian arrows would blot out the sun, the Spartan Dienekes replied that they would fight in the shade. The defiant last stand became a defining moment of Greek identity — proof that courage and discipline could transform defeat into moral victory.

The prescribed visual source for Spartan warfare — the bronze warrior figure from the British Museum (1929, 1016.6) — is a small bronze statuette of a Spartan soldier, leaning forward slightly as if about to advance. It is simple and austere, perfectly matching the Spartan self-image: no decoration, no ostentation, just readiness for battle. This material source complements the literary portrait of Spartan heroism that we find in Tyrtaeus and Herodotus.

The Greeks marked the site at Thermopylae with an inscription that became famous throughout the ancient world. The verse, attributed to the poet Simonides, declared that the dead lay here in obedience to the words of Sparta. The inscription made the site a permanent reminder of the values Tyrtaeus had preached: the obligation to die in one’s post rather than retreat. The Spartans were later celebrated with an annual festival at which boys competed in athletic contests, honouring the memory of those who fell. In Roman culture, Horace’s Ode 3.2 — another prescribed literary source — took this Spartan ideal and applied it to Roman citizens: dying for Rome is sweet and fitting, Horace writes, a sentiment that echoes Tyrtaeus across several centuries.

Roman Values of War: Virtue, Duty and Glory

Roman military values overlapped with Greek ones but had their own character. The Latin term virtus meant something like courage combined with excellence of character — the qualities that made a man capable of outstanding action. For Romans, virtus was demonstrated above all in war. A general who won a great victory could be awarded a triumph, the highest military honour: a procession through Rome to the Capitol at which the general rode in a chariot, his face painted red to resemble Jupiter, with his soldiers, captives and plunder parading behind him.

Roman literature also shaped and celebrated military values. Horace’s Ode 3.2, written under Augustus, tells Roman youths to harden themselves to war and endure hardship — the poem praises the man who dies for his country and condemns the coward who tries to live by dishonest means. Virgil’s Aeneid, also written in the Augustan period, presents Aeneas as the model Roman leader: pious, dutiful, restrained, willing to sacrifice personal happiness for the welfare of his people and for the destiny Rome must fulfil.

Key Fact

Roman values of war are expressed in two key literary sources: Horace’s Ode 3.2 praises dying for one’s country and condemns cowardice; Virgil’s Aeneid presents Aeneas as the ideal Roman leader — courageous, dutiful and self-sacrificing. Both poems were written in the reign of Augustus and helped define what Rome stood for.

Greek heroic culture, as expressed by Tyrtaeus, centred on individual honour (kleos, time) and the shame of surviving without it. The Spartan ideal pushed this to an extreme: only death in the front rank was truly honourable; any other outcome was degrading. Roman heroic culture, as expressed by Horace and Virgil, added the idea of collective duty to the state and to Rome’s divine destiny. Aeneas is not simply a brave warrior — he subordinates everything to the divine mission assigned to him. He weeps, suffers and sometimes wishes to die, but his commitment to duty (Latin: pietas) always prevails. This shift from personal glory to public duty is a meaningful difference between Greek and Roman heroic values, though both cultures agreed that the soldier who fought bravely and died well was the highest embodiment of their civic ideal.
